polityNote: Federal subjects of the Russian Federation from the dissolution of the USSR (26 Dec 1991) to the eve of the last merger (Zabaykalsky Krai, 1 Mar 2008, from which the present-day units are carried back). Atoms: geoBoundaries RUS ADM2 (OpenStreetMap/Wambacher 2017, 2,327 districts and urban okrugs, ODbL), assigned to subjects by the 2017 ADM1 layer of the same publisher (nested: each subject’s districts sum to its area within 0.8%). A subject is the union of its 2017 districts because no line between subjects moved between 1991 and 2017 except Moscow–Moscow Oblast (2012) and Chechnya–Ingushetia (fixed 2018); both are withheld. Autonomous okrugs are drawn as their own units from the Federation Treaty (31 Mar 1992) although formally inside their oblast or krai. State-border delimitations (China 2004/2008, Kazakhstan 2005) altered the outer line in places; the atoms carry the 2017 line. Check ① (2026-10-06): against the OpenHistoricalMap subjects in force on 2000-07-01 (0.05° grid, cos-weighted) the inland subjects agree at IoU 0.98–1.00 (Novosibirsk, Tomsk, Altai Krai, Buryatia, Komi, Kemerovo, Omsk, Kabardino-Balkaria, Jewish AO, Amur, Kaluga, Tula, Irkutsk, Agin-Buryat); coastal ones lie wholly inside OHM’s (≥0.997) whose outlines include the sea (IoU 0.79–0.95), and OHM draws Arkhangelsk, Tyumen and Kamchatka with their okrugs inside. Geodesic areas of okrug unions against the areas English Wikipedia states: Komi-Permyak 32,890 vs 32,770 km² (oldid 1376439141), Evenk 758,365 vs 767,600 (oldid 1374703454), Taymyr 838,255 vs 862,100 (oldid 1357085498; the Norilsk enclave is outside the union).
